facts.text: I have blisters on my skin, some small and some large.
They're itchy.
They're on my hands, my face, the back of my neck and my body.
They started on my hands and gradually spread to my face and body.
I've had them for 2 months.
I have a rash on my cheeks.
I have patchy skin lesions on my ears.
I have raw sores inside my cheeks, on the roof of my mouth and on my lips.
I've been losing hair.
I've lost weight.
My muscles ache.
I've been feeling tired.
I've been getting fevers.
They come and go.
I've had some nosebleeds; they stopped on their own.
I'm not short of breath.
I haven't seen any blood in my urine.
I'm not passing less urine than usual.
My muscles aren't weak.
I don't have any joint pain.
I haven't started any new medicines.
I'm Southeast Asian.

findings.name: skin examination
findings.result: Non-cicatricial hair loss; malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds; discoid lesions on the ears; numerous tense, clear vesicles and bullae on an erythematous base on the face, nape of the neck, trunk and hands.

findings.name: oral examination
findings.result: Superficial erosions on the buccal mucosa, hard palate and lips.

findings.name: general physical examination
findings.result: Apart from pallor and the skin, hair and mouth findings, the examination was unremarkable.

findings.name: liver function tests
findings.result: AST 194 U/L; ALT 53 U/L; albumin 2.9 g/L.

findings.name: urinalysis
findings.result: Active urinary sediment with white cells and albumin.

findings.name: peripheral blood smear
findings.result: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with pencil and teardrop cells.

gold.reasoning: 1. Bullous systemic lupus erythematosus was considered given underlying SLE manifestations and widespread tense vesicles and bullae — “Bullous systemic lupus erythematosus (BSLE) is a blistering disease characterized by tense subepidermal fluid‐filled vesicles and bullae. The common sites of involvement include the face, trunk, neck, extensor surfaces of upper limbs, and oral mucosa.” 2. Dermatitis herpetiformis was considered because of pruritic vesicles but is typically intensely pruritic on extensor surfaces rather than sun‐exposed skin — “Predilection to extensor surfaces, elbows, knees, and buttocks; intensely pruritic.” 3. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita was considered due to subepidermal blistering but usually occurs without SLE and heals with scarring — “Absence of SLE; heal with scarring and milia formation.” 4. Bullous pemphigoid was considered given tense bullae but often presents with eosinophil‐rich infiltrates and a prodrome of pruritus without mucosal involvement — “Prodrome of moderate to severe pruritus +/− urticarial, papular lesions; responsive to corticosteroids.” 5. Linear IgA bullous dermatosis was considered as it can mimic other bullous diseases but shows linear IgA deposition on split skin — “Linear deposition of IgA on the epidermal side of split skin. Resembles dermatitis herpetiformis.”

source_issues: s009: albumin 2.9 g/L is implausible as written (probably 2.9 g/dL).
s002 reports intermittent fever while s004 gives a normal temperature at the visit; not a contradiction for an intermittent symptom.
notes: Index visit: the presentation after 2 months of itchy blisters spreading from the hands to the face and trunk (s001-s008); the laboratory results (s009-s011) are findings from the same workup.

Signs the patient can notice (facial rash, ear lesions, mouth and lip sores, hair loss, blisters on the back of the neck) are facts in lay words and also stay in the examination findings; pallor and tachycardia are examiner findings only.
s008 'the remainder of the exam was unremarkable' is a general examination record (x011) whose result names what was abnormal elsewhere.
Gold aliases are lupus forms with blisters only; plain 'systemic lupus erythematosus' is broader and is left to the judge.
